claim: Mosquito immune cells, known as hemocytes, are integral to cellular and humoral responses that limit pathogen survival and mediate immune priming.
source: Mosquito immune cells, known as hemocytes, are integral to cellular and humoral responses that limit pathogen survival and mediate immune priming.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research (Baton et al., 2009; Castillo et al., 2017; Hillyer et al., 2003a; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016; Ramirez et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2010) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: Without reliable cell markers and genetic tools, studies of mosquito immune cells have been limited to morphological observations.
source: However, without reliable cell markers and genetic tools, studies of mosquito immune cells have been limited to morphological observations, leaving several aspects of their biology uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by general knowledge and the context of the study.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to characterize mosquito immune cells, demonstrating an increased complexity to previously defined prohemocyte, oenocytoid, and granulocyte subtypes.
source: Here, we use single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to characterize mosquito immune cells, demonstrating an increased complexity to previously defined prohemocyte, oenocytoid, and granulocyte subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including clustering analysis and functional assays.

claim: Functional assays relying on phagocytosis, phagocyte depletion, and RNA-FISH experiments define markers to accurately distinguish immune cell subtypes.
source: Through functional assays relying on phagocytosis, phagocyte depletion, and RNA-FISH experiments, we define markers to accurately distinguish immune cell subtypes and provide evidence for immune cell maturation and differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-FISH, phagocytosis assays, and clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 3 and related text.

claim: Gene-silencing experiments demonstrate the importance of lozenge in defining the mosquito oenocytoid cell fate.
source: In addition, gene-silencing experiments demonstrate the importance of lozenge in defining the mosquito oenocytoid cell fate.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments and qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Immune cells are vital to promoting wound healing, maintaining homeostasis, and providing anti-pathogen defenses across Metazoa.
source: Across Metazoa, immune cells are vital to promoting wound healing, maintaining homeostasis, and providing anti-pathogen defenses (Chaplin, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chaplin, 2010.

claim: Single-cell sequencing (scRNA-seq) has continued to delineate and provide further resolution into new cell types and immune cell functions in mammals.
source: Recently, the advent of single-cell sequencing (scRNA-seq) has continued to delineate and provide further resolution into new cell types and immune cell functions in mammals (Szabo et al., 2019; Villani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Szabo et al., 2019 and Villani et al., 2017.

claim: In lesser studied invertebrates lacking adaptive immunity, single-cell technologies have enhanced descriptions of previously described cell types and have redefined cell complexity.
source: In lesser studied invertebrates lacking adaptive immunity, single-cell technologies have enhanced descriptions of previously described cell types and have redefined cell complexity (Cattenoz et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2020; Raddi et al., 2020; Severo et al., 2018; Tattikota et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple recent studies (Cattenoz et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2020; Raddi et al., 2020; Severo et al., 2018; Tattikota et al., 2020).

claim: Hematopoiesis and immune cell function have predominantly been examined in Lepidoptera and Drosophila.
source: In insects, hematopoiesis and immune cell function have predominantly been examined in Lepidoptera and Drosophila (Banerjee et al., 2019; Lavine and Strand, 2002), with the mosquito, Anopheles gambiae, recently serving as an emerging study system (Kwon and Smith, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2019 and Lavine and Strand, 2002.

claim: Anopheles gambiae has recently served as an emerging study system for hematopoiesis and immune cell function.
source: In insects, hematopoiesis and immune cell function have predominantly been examined in Lepidoptera and Drosophila (Banerjee et al., 2019; Lavine and Strand, 2002), with the mosquito, Anopheles gambiae, recently serving as an emerging study system (Kwon and Smith, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kwon and Smith, 2019.

claim: Mosquito immune cells (hemocytes) have proven integral to the cellular and humoral responses that limit invading pathogens in the mosquito host.
source: Mosquito immune cells (hemocytes) have proven integral to the cellular and humoral responses that limit invading pathogens in the mosquito host (Baton et al., 2009; Castillo et al., 2017; Hillyer et al., 2003a; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016) and the establishment of immune memory (Ramirez et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Baton et al., 2009; Castillo et al., 2017; Hillyer et al., 2003a; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: Mosquito hemocytes are involved in the establishment of immune memory.
source: Mosquito immune cells (hemocytes) have proven integral to the cellular and humoral responses that limit invading pathogens in the mosquito host (Baton et al., 2009; Castillo et al., 2017; Hillyer et al., 2003a; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016) and the establishment of immune memory (Ramirez et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramirez et al., 2015 and Rodrigues et al., 2010.

claim: Transcriptional and proteomic analysis of mosquito hemocyte populations have yielded important information into the regulation of hemocyte function in response to blood-feeding and infection.
source: Transcriptional (Baton et al., 2009; Pinto et al., 2009) and proteomic (Smith et al., 2016) analysis of mosquito hemocyte populations have yielded important information into the regulation of hemocyte function in response to blood-feeding and infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baton et al., 2009; Pinto et al., 2009; and Smith et al., 2016.

claim: The study of mosquito immune cells has been complicated by discrepancies in cell classification.
source: However, the study of mosquito immune cells has been complicated by discrepancies in cell classification (Ribeiro and Brehélin, 2006), cell numbers (Hillyer and Strand, 2014), and methodologies to examine their function (Kwon and Smith, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ribeiro and Brehélin, 2006.

claim: Traditional classifications of mosquito hemocytes describe three cell types: prohemocyte precursors, phagocytic granulocytes, and oenocytoids that have primary roles in melanization.
source: Traditional classifications of mosquito hemocytes describe three cell types: prohemocyte precursors, phagocytic granulocytes, and oenocytoids that have primary roles in melanization (Castillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castillo et al., 2006.

claim: Recent studies have begun to challenge traditional immune cell classifications, demonstrating the existence of multiple types of phagocytic cells.
source: However, recent studies have begun to challenge these traditional immune cell classifications, demonstrating the existence of multiple types of phagocytic cells (Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018) and that both granulocytes and oenocytoids contribute to prophenoloxidase expression (Bryant and Michel, 2016; Kwon et al., 2020; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kwon and Smith, 2019 and Severo et al., 2018.

claim: Both granulocytes and oenocytoids contribute to prophenoloxidase expression.
source: However, recent studies have begun to challenge these traditional immune cell classifications, demonstrating the existence of multiple types of phagocytic cells (Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018) and that both granulocytes and oenocytoids contribute to prophenoloxidase expression (Bryant and Michel, 2016; Kwon et al., 2020; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bryant and Michel, 2016; Kwon et al., 2020; Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018; and Smith et al., 2016.

claim: There is additional complexity to mosquito immune cells that are not accurately represented by the traditional classification of mosquito hemocytes into three cell types.
source: Together, this suggests that there is additional complexity to mosquito immune cells that are not accurately represented by the traditional classification of mosquito hemocytes into three cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies that challenge traditional classifications.

claim: A total of 262 cells passed the quality filtering threshold of 10,000 reads per cell.
source: A total of 262 cells passed the quality filtering threshold of 10,000 reads per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), yielding 194 and 68 cells, respectively from naive and blood-fed conditions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 194 cells were obtained from naive conditions and 68 cells from blood-fed conditions.
source: A total of 262 cells passed the quality filtering threshold of 10,000 reads per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), yielding 194 and 68 cells, respectively from naive and blood-fed conditions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: Expression was detected from approximately 46% (6352/13,764) of the An. gambiae genome.
source: Overall, we detected expression (>0.1 RPKM) from ~46% (6352/13,764) of the An. gambiae genome, with a median of 1646 genes expressed per cell (range 45–5215), comparable to Severo et al., 2018.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with specific numbers provided.

claim: The median number of genes expressed per cell was 1646 (range 45–5215).
source: Overall, we detected expression (>0.1 RPKM) from ~46% (6352/13,764) of the An. gambiae genome, with a median of 1646 genes expressed per cell (range 45–5215), comparable to Severo et al., 2018.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: The data display a higher number of genes per cell and larger variance in genes between cell types compared to previous studies, suggesting a broader range of cell populations.
source: However, our data display a higher number of genes per cell and larger variance in genes between cell types, patterns suggestive of a broader range of cell populations represented in our dataset.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the authors' analysis of their data.

claim: Eight distinct cell clusters or immune cell-subtypes were conservatively defined using hierarchical clustering.
source: Using hierarchical clustering, we conservatively define eight distinct cell clusters or immune cell-subtypes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each cell cluster is represented in the all-inclusive gating condition (Gate 4).
source: When referenced to our FACS gating methodology based on WGA/DRAQ5 staining (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), each cell cluster is represented in our targeted, yet all-inclusive gating conditions (Gate 4), although these gating conditions (Gate 4) were only performed under naïve conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clusters 1, 7, and 8 are enriched in Gate 1.
source: Clusters 1, 7, and 8 are enriched in Gate 1, Clusters 5 and 6 in Gate 2, and Clusters 2–4 in Gate 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), arguing that these cells have similar physical properties in WGA staining and DNA content.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clusters 5 and 6 are enriched in Gate 2.
source: Clusters 1, 7, and 8 are enriched in Gate 1, Clusters 5 and 6 in Gate 2, and Clusters 2–4 in Gate 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), arguing that these cells have similar physical properties in WGA staining and DNA content.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clusters 2–4 are enriched in Gate 3.
source: Clusters 1, 7, and 8 are enriched in Gate 1, Clusters 5 and 6 in Gate 2, and Clusters 2–4 in Gate 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), arguing that these cells have similar physical properties in WGA staining and DNA content.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in DNA content amongst the FACS gating conditions are suggestive of potential variations in ploidy in hemocyte populations.
source: The differences in DNA content amongst the FACS gating conditions are suggestive of potential variations in ploidy (the number of sets of chromosomes) in hemocyte populations as previously suggested (Bryant and Michel, 2016; Bryant and Michel, 2014), although ploidy levels for individual hemocyte subtypes have not previously been described.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data, supported by citations to Bryant and Michel, 2016 and Bryant and Michel, 2014.

claim: With the exception of Cluster 3, each of the respective cell clusters were found under both naïve and blood-fed conditions.
source: With the exception of Cluster 3, which was only identified in naïve mosquitoes, each of the respective cell clusters were found under both naïve and blood-fed conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cluster 3 was only identified in naïve mosquitoes.
source: With the exception of Cluster 3, which was only identified in naïve mosquitoes, each of the respective cell clusters were found under both naïve and blood-fed conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only Clusters 2 and 4 displayed significant changes in gene expression between naive and blood-fed cells.
source: When paired with differential gene expression between naive and blood-fed cells of each cluster, only Clusters 2 and 4 displayed significant changes in gene expression (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Supplementary file 2.

claim: Cluster 2 shows down-regulation of several immune genes (TEP1, SCRASP1, and LYSC1) following blood-feeding.
source: Interestingly, this includes the down-regulation of several immune genes (TEP1, SCRASP1, and LYSC1) following blood-feeding in Cluster 2 that have previously defined roles in pathogen defense (Blandin et al., 2004; Kajla et al., 2011; Levashina et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2016), while genes involved in vesicle trafficking (Rab6A) and redox metabolism display increased expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and supported by citations.

claim: TEP1, SCRASP1, and LYSC1 have previously defined roles in pathogen defense.
source: Interestingly, this includes the down-regulation of several immune genes (TEP1, SCRASP1, and LYSC1) following blood-feeding in Cluster 2 that have previously defined roles in pathogen defense (Blandin et al., 2004; Kajla et al., 2011; Levashina et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2016), while genes involved in vesicle trafficking (Rab6A) and redox metabolism display increased expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blandin et al., 2004; Kajla et al., 2011; Levashina et al., 2001; and Smith et al., 2016.

claim: Genes involved in vesicle trafficking (Rab6A) and redox metabolism display increased expression in Cluster 2 following blood-feeding.
source: Interestingly, this includes the down-regulation of several immune genes (TEP1, SCRASP1, and LYSC1) following blood-feeding in Cluster 2 that have previously defined roles in pathogen defense (Blandin et al., 2004; Kajla et al., 2011; Levashina et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2016), while genes involved in vesicle trafficking (Rab6A) and redox metabolism display increased expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cluster 4 displayed an increase in gene expression for a serrate RNA effector molecule (Ars2), an integrin (AGAP006826), and a Sp2 transcription factor (AGAP004438) following blood-feeding.
source: Cluster 4 displayed an increase in gene expression for a serrate RNA effector molecule (Ars2), an integrin (AGAP006826), and a Sp2 transcription factor (AGAP004438) following blood-feeding, while an enzyme involved in the processing of glycoproteins (AGAP000249) was significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: An enzyme involved in the processing of glycoproteins (AGAP000249) was significantly reduced in Cluster 4 following blood-feeding.
source: Cluster 4 displayed an increase in gene expression for a serrate RNA effector molecule (Ars2), an integrin (AGAP006826), and a Sp2 transcription factor (AGAP004438) following blood-feeding, while an enzyme involved in the processing of glycoproteins (AGAP000249) was significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Blood-feeding may primarily influence the activation state and gene expression of specific immune cell subtypes.
source: Together, these data suggest that blood-feeding may primarily influence the activation state and gene expression of specific immune cell subtypes as previously suggested (Bryant and Michel, 2016; Bryant and Michel, 2014; Reynolds et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data, supported by citations to Bryant and Michel, 2016; Bryant and Michel, 2014; Reynolds et al., 2020; and Smith et al., 2016.

claim: No discernable differences in the expression of mitotic markers were detected between naive and blood-fed conditions.
source: When the expression of mitotic markers (Raddi et al., 2020) was examined under naive (sugar-fed) and blood-fed conditions, no discernable differences were detected between physiological conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Clusters 2 and 4 displayed the highest expression of mitotic markers.
source: Clusters 2 and 4 displayed the highest expression of mitotic markers (Figure 2C), supporting that these cells may have some capacity for proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Clusters 2 and 4 may have some capacity for proliferation.
source: Clusters 2 and 4 displayed the highest expression of mitotic markers (Figure 2C), supporting that these cells may have some capacity for proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of mitotic markers.

claim: Transcripts of Clusters 2–4 have the strongest associations with phagocytic immune cells based on correlations with a previous proteomics study.
source: Correlations with a previous proteomics study of phagocytic granulocytes in An. gambiae (Smith et al., 2016) demonstrate that transcripts of Clusters 2–4 have the strongest associations with phagocytic immune cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), providing support that these clusters represent populations of phagocytic granulocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2016.

claim: Clusters 2–4 represent populations of phagocytic granulocytes.
source: Correlations with a previous proteomics study of phagocytic granulocytes in An. gambiae (Smith et al., 2016) demonstrate that transcripts of Clusters 2–4 have the strongest associations with phagocytic immune cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), providing support that these clusters represent populations of phagocytic granulocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on correlations with previous proteomics data.

claim: Cells in Cluster 5 display a unique profile predominantly comprised of genes implicated in redox metabolism/stress responses.
source: Cells in Cluster 5 display a unique profile predominantly comprised of genes implicated in redox metabolism/stress responses (Figure 2D), while Clusters 7 and 8 display marked differences in composition (Figure 2D), despite sharing similar markers to delineate these cell types (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Clusters 7 and 8 display marked differences in composition despite sharing similar markers.
source: Cells in Cluster 5 display a unique profile predominantly comprised of genes implicated in redox metabolism/stress responses (Figure 2D), while Clusters 7 and 8 display marked differences in composition (Figure 2D), despite sharing similar markers to delineate these cell types (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2A and 2D.

claim: Cells of Cluster 1 likely represent non-hemocyte contaminating cells such as fat body or oenocytes.
source: Using the 'fat body' and 'muscle' enriched gene sets for An. gambiae defined by Raddi et al., 2020 and the 'non-hemocyte' gene set in Drosophila from Tattikota et al., 2020 for comparison to our cell clusters, we demonstrate that genes expressed in Cluster 1 closely resemble the profiles of non-hemocyte cell types and likely represents cellular debris (such as fat body or oenocytes) associated with perfusion techniques (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to Raddi et al., 2020 and Tattikota et al., 2020.

claim: The high DNA content of Cluster 1 cells supports that they may represent fat body cells or other polyploid cell types.
source: This is further supported by the high DNA content of Cluster 1 cells identified by our FACS methodology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), where previous studies in mosquitoes (Dittmann et al., 1989) and other insect species (Ren et al., 2020) have demonstrated that fat body cells display increased levels of cell ploidy.
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations to Dittmann et al., 1989 and Ren et al., 2020.

claim: SPARC and Cg25C were expressed at high levels across cell clusters, suggesting that these could be universally expressed markers of mosquito immune cells.
source: SPARC and Cg25C were expressed at high levels across cell clusters, suggesting that these could be universally expressed markers of mosquito immune cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Clusters 2–4 and 6 express the Drosophila plasmatocyte markers peroxidasin (pxn) and eater, suggestive of phagocytic cell function.
source: Clusters 2–4 and 6 express the Drosophila plasmatocyte markers (equivalent to mosquito granulocytes) peroxidasin (pxn) and eater (Figure 2E) suggestive of phagocytic cell function.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The expression of lozenge (lz) and PPO1 indicative of Drosophila crystal cells were most prevalent in Clusters 7 and 8.
source: In contrast, the expression of lozenge (lz) and PPO1 indicative of Drosophila crystal cells (Cattenoz et al., 2020; Dudzic et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2014; Fossett et al., 2003; Tattikota et al., 2020) were most prevalent in Clusters 7 and 8 (Figure 2E), suggesting that these cell clusters are representative of mosquito oenocytoid populations (equivalent to crystal cells).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2E, and supported by citations.

claim: Clusters 7 and 8 are representative of mosquito oenocytoid populations.
source: In contrast, the expression of lozenge (lz) and PPO1 indicative of Drosophila crystal cells (Cattenoz et al., 2020; Dudzic et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2014; Fossett et al., 2003; Tattikota et al., 2020) were most prevalent in Clusters 7 and 8 (Figure 2E), suggesting that these cell clusters are representative of mosquito oenocytoid populations (equivalent to crystal cells).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression and comparison to Drosophila.

claim: NimB2 and PPO6 support their use as universal markers of mosquito immune cells.
source: As previously suggested (Kwon and Smith, 2019), the expression of NimB2 and PPO6 support their use as universal markers of mosquito immune cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2F, and supported by a citation to Kwon and Smith, 2019.

claim: The expression of LRIM16A, LRR8, and LYS I in cells of Clusters 2–4 and 6 suggest that these cells are granulocytes in origin.
source: The expression of LRIM16A, LRR8, and LYS I in cells of Clusters 2–4 and 6 suggest that these cells are granulocytes in origin (Raddi et al., 2020; Severo et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016), while the expression of SCRASP1, SRPN10, and LRIM15 (Danielli et al., 2003; Smith et al., 2016) in Clusters 2–4 suggest that these are more specialized granulocyte populations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2F, and supported by citations.

claim: The expression of SCRASP1, SRPN10, and LRIM15 in Clusters 2–4 suggest that these are more specialized granulocyte populations.
source: The expression of LRIM16A, LRR8, and LYS I in cells of Clusters 2–4 and 6 suggest that these cells are granulocytes in origin (Raddi et al., 2020; Severo et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016), while the expression of SCRASP1, SRPN10, and LRIM15 (Danielli et al., 2003; Smith et al., 2016) in Clusters 2–4 suggest that these are more specialized granulocyte populations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2F, and supported by citations.

claim: PPO6 is universally expressed in all hemocytes.
source: As previously suggested (Kwon and Smith, 2019; Severo et al., 2018), PPO6 is universally expressed in all hemocytes (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2F and 2G, and supported by citations.

claim: PPO2, PPO4, PPO5, and PPO9 are most abundant in putative granulocyte populations.
source: PPO2, PPO4, PPO5, and PPO9 are most abundant in putative granulocyte populations, while PPO1, PPO3, and PPO8 are enriched in putative oenocytoids (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: PPO1, PPO3, and PPO8 are enriched in putative oenocytoids.
source: PPO2, PPO4, PPO5, and PPO9 are most abundant in putative granulocyte populations, while PPO1, PPO3, and PPO8 are enriched in putative oenocytoids (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The data contrast previous suggestions that mosquito PPOs are only constitutively expressed in oenocytoid populations.
source: This directly contrasts previous suggestions that mosquito PPOs are only constitutively expressed in oenocytoid populations (Castillo et al., 2006; Hillyer and Strand, 2014; Strand, 2008), yet is supported by recent evidence that phagocytic granulocyte populations in mosquitoes significantly contribute to PPO production (Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to previous and recent studies.

claim: Phagocytic granulocyte populations in mosquitoes significantly contribute to PPO production.
source: This directly contrasts previous suggestions that mosquito PPOs are only constitutively expressed in oenocytoid populations (Castillo et al., 2006; Hillyer and Strand, 2014; Strand, 2008), yet is supported by recent evidence that phagocytic granulocyte populations in mosquitoes significantly contribute to PPO production (Kwon and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kwon and Smith, 2019 and Smith et al., 2016.

claim: Known anti-microbial genes and signaling components of the Toll, IMD, and JAK-STAT pathways display the highest expression in Clusters 2 and 8.
source: We demonstrate that known anti-microbial genes and signaling components of the Toll, IMD, and JAK-STAT pathways (Cirimotich et al., 2010) display the highest expression in Clusters 2 and 8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), similar to the expression patterns of SRPNs and CLIPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) that mediate immune activation (Gulley et al., 2013; Kanost and Jiang, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4, and supported by citations.

claim: Mosquito granulocyte and oenocytoid populations each contribute to the expression of a distinct subset of immune signaling processes.
source: This suggests that mosquito granulocyte and oenocytoid populations each contribute to the expression of a distinct subset of immune signaling processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: Receptors involved in chemosensory recognition are highly expressed in Clusters 7 and 8.
source: Interestingly, receptors involved in chemosensory recognition (ionotropic, gustatory, and odorant receptors; odorant binding proteins) are highly expressed in Clusters 7 and 8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The role of odorant binding proteins on immune system development has been described previously in other insect systems.
source: Although their function has not been described in mosquitoes, the role of odorant binding proteins on immune system development has been described previously in other insect systems (Benoit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benoit et al., 2017.

claim: NimB2, SPARC, and PPO6 are universal markers of mosquito immune cell populations.
source: Based on these characterizations, our data support the identification of NimB2, SPARC, and PPO6 as universal markers of mosquito immune cell populations that can be found in each of our cell clusters (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Cluster 5 represents a progenitor population of prohemocytes.
source: Given the low number of expressed genes (Figure 1), the lack of discernable markers (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 8), and low levels of cyclin G2 (Supplementary file 5) that define differentiated cell populations (Horne et al., 1997; Martínez-Gac et al., 2004), we believe that Cluster 5 represents a progenitor population of prohemocytes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and supported by citations.

claim: Clusters 2–4 and 6 can be described as granulocytes, distinguished by LRIM16A and LRR8.
source: Clusters 2–4 and 6 can be described as granulocytes, distinguished by LRIM16A and LRR8 (Raddi et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2016), and further delineated as 'mature' granulocyte populations in Clusters 2–4 marked by the expression of LRIM15 and SCRASP1 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 8, and supported by citations.

claim: Clusters 2–4 represent 'mature' granulocyte populations marked by the expression of LRIM15 and SCRASP1.
source: Clusters 2–4 and 6 can be described as granulocytes, distinguished by LRIM16A and LRR8 (Raddi et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2016), and further delineated as 'mature' granulocyte populations in Clusters 2–4 marked by the expression of LRIM15 and SCRASP1 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Cluster 6 likely represents immature granulocytes.
source: In the absence of these additional phagocytic markers, we believe that the less defined populations of Cluster 6 likely represent immature granulocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of mature granulocyte markers.

claim: Clusters 7 and 8 represent populations of oenocytoids that can be denoted by the expression of SCRB9 and SCRB3.
source: Clusters 7 and 8 represent populations of oenocytoids that can easily be denoted by the expression of two scavenger receptors, SCRB9 and SCRB3 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The 'universal' marker Nimrod B2 (NimB2) labeled all hemocytes.
source: Supported by our expression data, the 'universal' marker Nimrod B2 (NimB2) labeled all hemocytes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LRIM15 effectively labels phagocytic cell populations.
source: Serving as a marker for phagocytic cells, we demonstrate that LRIM15 effectively labels phagocytic cell populations (Figure 3B), while the labeling of SCRB9 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and SCRB3 denote mosquito oenocytoid populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SCRB9 and SCRB3 denote mosquito oenocytoid populations.
source: Serving as a marker for phagocytic cells, we demonstrate that LRIM15 effectively labels phagocytic cell populations (Figure 3B), while the labeling of SCRB9 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and SCRB3 denote mosquito oenocytoid populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNA-FISH experiments with both LRIM15 and SCRB9 probes identify distinct populations of LRIM15+ or SCRB9+ cells.
